newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Shady Tirana boulevard is childrens' peace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Shady Tirana boulevard is childrens' peace.

text.p: When the heat of the sun has subsided, children start climbing up the pyramid walls of the cultural centre -- formerly a museum to the life of communist dictator Enver Hoxha -- and slide down its smooth surface.

Those whose parents have a spare 30 leks (about 17 U.S. cents) get dizzy on a single fairground ride while their parents eat ice cream and chat -- about family, friends, the elections due later this month.

Teenagers bustle and preen in brand new jeans, showing off designer belts. Older people watch, or promenade sedately past street vendors offering bathroom scales to weigh them, a swirling chair for shoeshine, cigarettes, a mobile phone.

This is Albania too. In the shade of Bulevardi (Boulevard), the safest street in the capital of a country riven by chaos and violence, people are keeping alive their social traditions: walking about, greeting friends with a caress on the cheek.
"Over here it looks as if nothing bad is happening -- it's total peace and fun," said the man running the flying car ride as he hit the "up" button.
"Business is going very well, it's a surprise for foreigners. In this corner here life goes on, it looks like another world. But I don't understand it myself."

Whatever the appearances here, people sense it could take very little to rekindle the violence that ripped through Europe's poorest country earlier this year. Even the capital's main street is a precarious paradise.
FEAR AND RUMOUR FILL THE CAPITAL

"It's true we're coming out to take the children but we're still afraid; with every day the election nears the more afraid we are," said 40-year-old Violeta, sitting with her friend Agetina as their children scaled the pyramid.

Central Tirana was not immune to mass unrest caused by the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes across Albania in March, with rioting crowds damaging some buildings. But it came off much more lightly than some places outside the capital.

As night falls the crowds will disperse: people need to be sure they are home in good time for curfew hours when the rattle of machine gun fire will disturb their children's sleep as it does every night. Only recently there was an explosion in a cafe nearby.
Anxiety mounts as the time nears when they should be off the streets for fear anyone, in uniform or not, could shoot them.
"At least in war you know it's there," said 18-year-old Enis, sitting with his armed friends under a straw-roofed bar in the labyrinth of cafes that has filled the former main park.

Until curfew in the heart of Tirana -- a group of young boys staying away from school say it is the only half-safe part of town -- one can try to take Albania's feeble political pulse ahead of the June 29 poll aimed at restoring order.
What emerges are individuals still coming to terms with broad freedoms in the almost seven years since Albania's peculiarly paranoid brand of communist isolation fell away.
Physically crumbling, Tirana is shot through with fear, gangland law, rumours and conspiracy theories.
Fuelled partly by daily word of corruption, one of the stories doing the rounds is "there has been an envelope" that people claim to have seen, holding the results of the election.
MAKE MONEY, HAVE COFFEE, HAVE A GOOD TIME
Back in the bar there is no consensus even among the five young men, hanging out more or less together, drinking cola.

A very casual straw poll of who will win the election -- the rightist Democratic Party headed by current President Sali Berisha, or Socialists under Fatos Nano -- produced just a slim three to two vote in favour of the Socialists.

"People want to express themselves," said Genci, 27, a sharp-nosed passionate pro-Democrat. But he rejected either parties' opposing campaigning slogans, linking the Socialists with communism or the Democrats with dictatorship.
"The problem in Albania is that those that get powerful just concentrate on getting rich," he said. "As Albanians we just want to make money, have coffee and have a good time."
One of youths offered a gun for $400, but found no takers.
The early evening feels calm as you stroll past Bar Romantik.
Back out on Bulevardi proper, cars carving a route through the dust are the only obvious nuisance scattering pedestrians on their ritual evening parade.
A second-hand bookseller is offering "Frojd" -- a book about Sigmund Freud in Albanian.
FROM THE CRACK OF GUNS TO THE BARKING OF DOGS

Some roads within and beyond Tirana are lethal, and Bulevardi can be a deadly trigger-happy corridor around curfew at 10 p.m. But, for Genci at least, Albania's violence is merely about "someone having a bone to pick with someone else".
Political ideology is not something many people here, after almost 50 years with only images of Hoxha on offer for spiritual inspiration, seem to be moved by.

"All of the politicians are just fighting for their own chairs," said Agetina back at the pyramid, loudly "shushed" by her companion, as children gathered round. "I'm not trusting anyone -- I'm just going to cross out everybody on the paper."

"I don't know about the elections," said Gazmir, a young policeman who has spent a month standing to attention in the sun armed with a gun to shoot any Bulevardi troublemakers. "It seems to me all these cities want to topple the president."
Tirana residents seem not to come to Bulevardi to get heated about things.
Eventually, on Tirana nights, the gunfire tends to give way to the more common southern European sound of baying dogs.
"When someone doesn't have any money I just let him ride for free," says the man with the fairground ride.
"In the end it's the children," he said. "You're supposed to be nice to children."
